newsitem.title: INDIA: India relaxes rules for financial services sector.
newsitem.headline: India relaxes rules for financial services sector.

text.p: India on Tuesday formally announced equity levels for foreign investors in non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) in a bid to usher in transparency and woo foreign funds to its financial sector.
The Finance Ministry in a statement outlined minimum levels of investment pegged to the extent of foreign equity participation.

"The government has for the first time formally announced the guidelines. The cut-off levels have been fixed to keep away non-serious players," a finance ministry official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

The Finance Ministry said in a statement that foreign investment would be permitted in a host of financial services including merchant banking, underwriting, portfolio management services, financial consultancy, stockbroking, asset management, venture capital firms, and credit rating agencies.
"There is more transparency now and this will help to attract foreign capital," Vipin Aggarwal, chief dealer at DBS Capital Trust Securities Pvt Ltd, a securities firm, told Reuters.
Earlier very few foreign firms could venture into non-banking services as the guidelines were not very clear, Aggarwal said.
"The guidelines announced are in line with the liberalisation policy and will boost foreign investment," he added.
India opened up its financial sector as part of economic reforms launched in 1991 after decades of socialist control.

The Finance Ministry said the minimum capitalisation would be $500,000 in NBFCs where foreign equity was 51 percent or less, $5.0 million in NBFCs where foreign equity was more than 51 percent but less than or equal to 75 percent, and $50 million in NBFCs where foreign equity was more than 75 percent.
It said 100 percent foreign-owned NBFCs would be required to act as holding companies, with specific activities undertaken by subsidiaries with a minimum domestic equity of 25 percent.
The ministry said for foreign equity holdings between 75 and 100 percent, capitalisation would need to be $7.5 million up-front with the balance to be brought in over 24 months.
Earlier for foreign equity holdings between 75 and 100 percent, the capitalisation needed was $5.0 million, the finance ministry official said.
For subsidiaries of 100 percent foreign-owned NBFCs, domestic equity amounting to 10 percent would have to be up-front with the balance domestic equity to be introduced over a period of 24 months.
"All proposals for foreign equity investment in NBFCs will be considered by the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB)," the statement said.
The FIPB is a panel of senior government officials attached to the Industry Ministry which can approve foreign investment up to six billion rupees ($167.6 million).
